summary: The TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator works out TTM last reported quarter. It uses the TTM one quarter before, the TTM two quarters before, the revenue last reported quarter and the revenue one quarter before. That makes it useful for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator work?
sections.html:
The TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports TTM last reported quarter in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the TTM mode); then you type in the TTM one quarter before, the TTM two quarters before, the revenue last reported quarter and the revenue one quarter before.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

TTM last reported quarter=trailing twelve month value − TTM one quarter before − TTM two quarters before − TTM three quarters before
Revenue three quarters before=revenue TTM − revenue last reported quarter − revenue one quarter before − revenue two quarters before
EPS two quarters before=earnings per share TTM − EPS last reported quarter − EPS one quarter before − EPS three quarters before
TTM last reported quarter=-TTM one quarter before − TTM two quarters before − TTM three quarters before + yield TTM × current stock price × outstanding shares
EV / EBITDA TTM=enterprise value ÷ (EBITDA last reported quarter + EBITDA one quarter before + EBITDA two quarters before + EBITDA three quarters before)
EPS two quarters before=-EPS last reported quarter − EPS one quarter before − EPS three quarters before + current stock price ÷ price to earnings TTM

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take TTM mode set to Original TTM mode, TTM one quarter before = 10, TTM two quarters before = 10 and TTM three quarters before = 10. The calculator returns TTM last reported quarter = -20.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: TTM last reported quarter = -20 should be roughly the size you expected from TTM mode set to Original TTM mode and TTM one quarter before = 10.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the TTM one quarter before, the TTM two quarters before and the revenue last reported quarter — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns TTM last reported quarter, derived from the TTM one quarter before, the TTM two quarters before and the revenue last reported quarter. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the TTM one quarter before, the TTM two quarters before, the revenue last reported quarter and the revenue one quarter before, which is 21 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter TTM last reported quarter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. TTM last reported quarter opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports TTM last reported quarter = -20. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the TTM (trailing twelve months) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
